fixes.explanation: Mercy, baker. Paul says God saved us, “…but according to His mercy…” That's what the saving rests on, not on anything we did. I'm glad, because my edges were never going to carry it.
That's right, baker. Paul says God saved us through “…the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.” The renewing is the Spirit's work. Nobody has to do it themselves.
Eternal life, baker. Paul says we would become “…heirs with the hope of eternal life.” And he says we're justified by God's grace, so it's a gift, not a paycheck.

True, baker. Paul says to avoid “…foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless.” He says it plainly. He doesn't soften it, so neither will I.

True, baker. Paul says such a man is “…corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.” That line comes right after he says to reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition. It's a heavier line in the letter, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.

Equip, baker. Paul says, “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.” The goal is that they have everything they need. I like a plan where nobody lacks anything.

That's it, baker. Paul says our people must devote themselves to good works “…in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful.” The good works are aimed at the needs in front of them. The focus is on the people in need.

Keeping your distance sounds smart, like parking in the back row so nobody notices you. But Paul doesn't say hide. He says to “…submit to rulers and authorities…” The same verse also says to be “…obedient and ready for every good work…”

Questioning every order is the coworker who wants a meeting about every single email. Paul's word is different: “…submit to rulers and authorities…” Then he adds that believers should be “…obedient and ready for every good work…” That's a lot of readiness for somebody who wants a debate first.

Strict and watchful sounds like a security guard squinting at everyone who walks by. Paul's words are softer. He wants believers to be “…peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone.” Relax the squint, friend.
Traditions of the elders aren't mentioned in this part of the letter. Paul says we were “…enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures…” That's the thing he names.

I understand the pull. Good deeds feel like they should count for a lot. But Paul says it the other way: “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy…” So the statement is false, and mercy is the reason.

False is right, friend. Paul writes, “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy…” So God saved us according to His mercy, and nobody has to pretend they earned it.
Temple priests don't show up anywhere in this passage, friend, so you can cross them off the guest list. Paul says it's “…renewal by the Holy Spirit.” The Spirit is the one who does the renewing.
A promised land is a fair guess, since heirs usually get handed something you can stand on. But Paul says we would become “…heirs with the hope of eternal life.” The hope he names is eternal life.

Good deeds, baker. Paul says he wants this stressed “…so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds.” Notice who it's for: those who have believed God. Belief and doing good go together here.

Long debates don't make Paul's list of things to devote yourself to. A moment later he says to avoid “…foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law…” What he wants those who have believed God to devote themselves to is “…good deeds.”

Test sounds like Paul wants to check Zenas and Apollos over. Paul's word is different: “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.” The goal is that they have everything they need.
